facts.learnerText: A base layer is worn underneath your hockey gear.
Your knee rests inside the cup at the top of a shin pad.

sourceRefs.section: Fit description: knee in centre donut

facts.learnerText: Hockey gloves cover your hands while you hold your stick.

sourceRefs.section: Fit guide: fingers, wrist and stick grip

facts.learnerText: Hockey pants sit around your hips and overlap your knee pads.
facts.applicationPrompt: Place the pants on the player.

sourceRefs.section: What a good fit looks like

facts.learnerText: Shoulder pads go over your head and rest on your shoulders.

sourceRefs.section: Fit description: head opening and shoulder placement

facts.learnerText: Smoothing the wrinkles in your hockey socks helps keep them comfortable.
A helmet is part of a hockey player's equipment.
facts.applicationPrompt: Find the helmet for your bag.

facts.learnerText: Skates are part of both a skater's and a goalie's hockey equipment.

sourceRefs.section: Player and goalie equipment lists: Skates

facts.learnerText: A goalie stick has a wider paddle and blade than a player's stick.
Your hockey bag carries your equipment, including gloves, skates and a helmet.
A practice jersey belongs in your hockey equipment checklist.
Two blue lines divide a full rink into three zones.
Boards surround the ice.
The centre circle is in the middle of a full rink.
The centre line is the red line across the middle.
On a marked full rink, the crease is the blue area in front of the goal.
The crossbar joins the tops of the goalposts.
Goalposts are the upright sides of the goal frame.
Your defensive zone is the end where your team protects its goal.
The neutral zone lies between the blue lines.
End boards are behind the goals.
A goalie wears the blocker on the stick hand.
A goalie wears the catching glove on the hand that does not hold the stick.
A full-strength NHL forward line has a centre and two wingers.
Moving into open space can give the puck carrier a passing option.
conditions: The passing route must be available.

facts.learnerText: Attackers look for time and space; defenders try to reduce both.
Puck support matters in your own end, through the middle and in attack.
An attacker can move between lanes to find open ice.

sourceRefs.section: Filling lanes and attacking with layers

facts.learnerText: Moving across the ice can help create a passing option.
conditions: The defender can still close the route.

facts.learnerText: Changing speed can help a puck carrier respond to the defence.
A small-area game uses part of the ice for a hockey game.
Hockey Canada's U7 program introduces hockey through fun and basic skills.
Hockey Canada's U9 half-ice model does not stop play for offside.
Hockey Canada's U9 guidance gives every player opportunities to try goalie.

sourceRefs.section: Are all players given the opportunity to play goalie?

facts.learnerText: A faceoff starts or resumes play with an official dropping the puck between opponents.
conditions: Applies where the competition uses faceoffs.

facts.learnerText: At a faceoff, the puck must touch the ice before players play it.
Under full-ice rules, periods and play after a goal begin with a centre faceoff.
conditions: Do not apply to small-ice programs with different restarts.

facts.learnerText: A puck that leaves the playing area causes a stoppage.
conditions: Do not infer the next faceoff location or a penalty.

facts.learnerText: An attacking teammate entering the attacking zone ahead of the puck can cause offside.
conditions: Controlled backward entry and defending-team puck returns have exceptions.
Needs a reviewed exact freeze and current rules before any question.

facts.learnerText: A puck bouncing off a skate is different from a deliberate kick.
conditions: This statement alone does not decide whether a goal counts.
